question: A 3-year-old girl with no significant past medical history presents to the clinic with a 4-day history of acute onset cough. Her parents have recently started to introduce several new foods into her diet. Her vital signs are all within normal limits. Physical exam is significant for decreased breath sounds on the right. What is the most appropriate definitive management in this patient?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Acute onset cough" -> "Decreased breath sounds on the right" -> "Possible foreign body aspiration" -> "Rigid bronchoscopy" -> 95%
CHAIN: "Acute onset cough" -> "Decreased breath sounds on the right" -> "Possible foreign body aspiration" -> "Flexible bronchoscopy" -> 70%
CHAIN: "Acute onset cough" -> "Decreased breath sounds on the right" -> "Possible foreign body aspiration" -> "Chest x-ray (CXR)" -> 60%
CHAIN: "Acute onset cough" -> "Decreased breath sounds on the right" -> "Possible asthma exacerbation" -> "Inhaled bronchodilators and oral corticosteroids" -> 50%
CHAIN: "Acute onset cough" -> "Decreased breath sounds on the right" -> "Possible pneumonia" -> "Empiric antibiotic therapy" -> 40%
analysis: The clinical presentation suggests a possible foreign body aspiration, given the acute onset of cough and decreased breath sounds on the right side, especially in the context of recent introduction of new foods. In such cases, rigid bronchoscopy is the most appropriate definitive management as it allows for both diagnosis and removal of the foreign body.
